title: Research and analysis of automotive half shaft remanufacturing assessment and carbon footprint accounting
content:
Abstract

Automotive half-shaft remanufacturing serves as a pivotal strategy for sustainable manufacturing, though comprehensive assessments of its structural reliability and ecological advantages are still lacking. This research tackles two critical gaps: (1) devising a non-destructive defect identification technique utilizing modal analysis, and (2) conducting a comparative carbon footprint analysis between remanufactured and newly produced components. Experimental findings reveal that natural frequency reduction correlates strongly with crack depth and positioning, with higher-order modes demonstrating superior damage sensitivity—a breakthrough for flaw categorization. Moreover, the developed lifecycle carbon model pinpoints material production (contributing 50% of total emissions) and heat treatment as the most emission-intensive stages in conventional manufacturing. Remanufacturing achieves 30–40% emission reductions, predominantly via material recycling. The innovative quantification framework, incorporating material flows, energy consumption, and waste emissions, establishes the first empirically verified model specific to half-shaft remanufacturing. This study not only refines structural diagnostics but also delivers actionable data to guide automotive circular economy policies.
